One-sentence judgment: coin, vending, and amusement machine servicers and repairers do not just restock and collect money, but install, maintain, adjust, or repair coin machines, vending machines, and amusement equipment (including electronic games, jukeboxes, pinball machines, and slot machines): O*NET defines this occupation as "install, service, adjust, or repair coin, vending, and amusement machines, including electronic games, jukeboxes, pinball machines, and slot machines", and this page follows the exact occupation basis of O*NET-SOC 49-9091.00.

Signals for continued exploration: you are willing to travel on site between several business locations and to both judge faults independently and reconcile records against money and merchandise; O*NET work context shows 84% have a great deal of freedom to make decisions, 85% use email every day, 53% communicate by telephone every day, 36% are in continuous contact with others, and 51% work more than 40 hours per week; work activities are led by repairing and maintaining mechanical equipment, performing general physical activities, documenting and recording information, and getting information.

Conditions for pausing high investment first: you have not yet completed one full closed loop of installation and wiring, inspection and testing, fault diagnosis and on-the-spot repair, records and reconciliation, and escalation when beyond capability, and you have not checked the local and enterprise authority and compliance requirements for electrical work, water and power connections, and equipment installation and transport; this occupation's preparation level is Job Zone 1-2 (little or some preparation), SVP below 6.0, and the education distribution on the page shows 92% of respondents answering that a high school diploma or equivalent is required, 8% answering that a postsecondary certificate is required, and 1% answering that an associate's or other two-year degree is required (the page shows only these three bands); this page does not infer personal hiring probability from that.

Education, training, certification, and position authorization must be checked separately: O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone 1-2 (little or some preparation), SVP below 6.0; the page provides 2 national certifications (the National Automatic Merchandising Association's NAMA Certified Executive and ETA International's Gaming and Vending Technician), but certification does not equal a license or an employer authorization, and does not equal a legal qualification for electrical work or water and power hookups; the water and power connections needed at installation must follow the applicable codes, and electrical work, transport, and site access must be checked item by item against the applicable jurisdiction and employer rules; this page describes tasks and boundaries based on O*NET and public sources and does not write education or certification as a legal qualification.

In one sentence: this is an occupation where whether the on-site judgment is accurate, whether wiring and installation comply, and whether money, merchandise, and records reconcile determine success more than speed of repair; if you are willing to leave a reviewable record for every on-site job you do, it is worth serious consideration.

The work of coin, vending, and amusement machine servicers and repairers can be divided into three connected but independent work surfaces. The first is installation, restocking, and collection: transport the machine to the installation site and make the necessary water and electrical connections to code, replenish merchandise, ingredients, money, and other consumables, collect coins and bills from the machine and issue invoices and settle accounts with the franchise operator, and keep records of delivered merchandise and collected money. The second is inspection and fault handling: check the machine and metering devices to determine the cause of a fault, handle small problems such as jammed bills or stuck merchandise, test the machine to confirm normal function, adjust and repair coin machines, vending machines, amusement equipment, and metering devices and replace faulty mechanical and electrical parts (using hand tools, soldering irons, and drawings), replace faulty parts (such as a worn magnetic head on an automated teller machine card reader), clean and oil machine parts, adjust machine pressure gauges and thermostats, and disassemble and assemble machines to specification with hand and power tools. The third is records and external coordination: keep machine maintenance and repair records, record transaction information on forms or in logs and notify designated personnel of discrepancies, contact other repair personnel or arrange machine removal when major repair is needed, order parts needed for machine repair, consult manuals and wiring diagrams for the information needed for repair, and travel on site to provide maintenance and repair service.

Safety and equipment and fund records come first, and stop and escalate when beyond capability and authority. US 1910.333 covers exposure to electrical hazards: in principle energy is disconnected first, and special conditions without de-energization are verified by the employer and still carry safety procedures, so testing is not automatically exempt. If de-energization was not locked or tagged through procedure, the circuit is still treated as energized, and a qualified person must verify that it cannot restart and test to confirm no voltage including backfeed or induced voltage; exposure to a circuit not de-energized is handled only by a qualified person with the required protection. An ordinary repair title does not automatically confer electrical qualification; re-energization follows the qualified person procedure with verification of tools and devices and clearing and notification of personnel, and normal function does not directly grant authority to energize. US 1910.147 covers maintenance and servicing that could cause injury from unexpected startup, energization, or release of stored energy, with applicable conditions and exceptions for normal production; electrical hazards are checked separately against 333, and an authorized employee must have procedure training for the actual duties. Stored energy may be eliminated, disconnected, restrained, or made safe, and it is not uniformly verified as zero energy; a stop button is not an isolation device, and de-energization and re-energization clearing and notification are verified through the actual procedure, and re-energization authority is not granted by an anomaly disappearing. The NIOSH general risk guidance supports assessment of force, repetition, posture, and intensity, frequency, and duration, and is not an occupational incidence rate or personal diagnosis; elimination, substitution, and engineering changes to tools and workstations come first, with task rotation, rest, and training as management supplements, and PPE cannot replace engineering controls; handling methods are assessed against the actual weight, route, tools, and personnel, and no uniform load or rest duration is given. Editorial record check: record merchandise, money, and transaction information separately according to the real enterprise's collection, counting, settlement, and discrepancy notification procedures; counting in person and registering the same day can serve as suggestions pending verification and are not a time limit set by O*NET or uniform regulations.

paragraphs: The six directions share part of their abilities with this occupation: mechanical and electrical common sense, troubleshooting thinking, measurement and test running habits, and on-site safety and record awareness. The real difference lies in the object and the responsibility: office equipment operators mainly operate equipment and handle routine matters, motor and tool repairers mainly overhaul motors themselves, mobile heavy equipment mechanics deal with construction machinery, appliance repairers provide in-home service for household appliances, machinery maintenance workers mainly do scheduled servicing, and safety and fire protection system installers mainly install and commission systems, while this occupation installs, services, and repairs commercial coin, vending, and amusement equipment and is also responsible for the flow of money and merchandise. When choosing, it is better to first verify with a deliverable troubleshooting and installation wiring exercise than to compare names.

The comparison basis is the tasks, work activities, and work context description on the O*NET-SOC 49-9091.00 page, the adjacent occupation list and common position titles on that page, the adjacent occupation slug list registered in this evidence route, and the public occupational materials of each adjacent occupation; the comparison is an editorial compilation and does not constitute a position authorization or a mutual recognition of qualifications conclusion.

The table below compares positions and occupations adjacent to this occupation: office equipment operators (except computer), motor and power tool repairers, mobile heavy equipment mechanics, appliance repairers, machinery maintenance workers, and safety and fire protection system installers. The four columns respectively answer the same kinds of questions: what this direction does, where the key difference from this occupation lies, and what kind of person is better suited to choose it.

Office equipment operators (except computer) mainly use and routinely operate office equipment; this occupation requires independently diagnosing faults, replacing parts, installing and wiring, and handling the money flow.
People willing to operate equipment daily and handle front desk matters suit that direction; people willing to travel on site and repair machines independently suit this occupation.
Mainly equipment operation and routine matter records.
Office equipment operators (except computer)

Motor and power tool repairers deal with the repair of motors and power tools, with work concentrated on the motor itself; this occupation deals with complete machines and also carries installation, restocking, and collection.
People willing to overhaul motors and tools themselves suit that direction; people willing to face complete machines, sites, and money responsibility suit this occupation.
Mainly motor and tool overhaul and trial run records.
Motor and power tool repairers

Mobile heavy equipment mechanics deal with the repair of construction and transport machinery, with a heavier working environment and mainly hydraulic and power systems; this occupation's equipment is smaller but the sites are more dispersed and involve money and merchandise.
People willing to repair heavy machinery and hydraulic systems suit that direction; people willing to provide on-site service for light commercial equipment suit this occupation.
Mainly heavy equipment repair and maintenance records.
Mobile heavy equipment mechanics

Appliance repairers deal with household appliances and work in the user's home, usually charging per item; this occupation deals with commercial coin, vending, and amusement equipment and serves along a site route.
People willing to do in-home repair of household appliances suit that direction; people willing to do route-based service for commercial equipment suit this occupation.
Mainly appliance repair and in-home service records.
Appliance repairers

Machinery maintenance workers mainly do scheduled servicing, lubrication, and inspection of equipment, do not handle money or merchandise, and do not carry installation wiring; this occupation also carries fault repair and record-to-physical consistency.
People willing to do scheduled servicing and work order execution suit that direction; people willing to diagnose faults independently and carry accounting responsibility suit this occupation.
Mainly servicing, inspection, and work order records.
Machinery maintenance workers

Safety and fire protection system installers deal with the installation and commissioning of safety and fire protection systems, with stricter compliance and acceptance requirements; this occupation's equipment leans more toward commercial self-service and amusement equipment.
People willing to do system installation, commissioning, and acceptance suit that direction; people willing to provide on-site service for commercial equipment suit this occupation.
Mainly system installation, commissioning, and acceptance records.
Safety and fire protection system installers

Moving from this occupation to an adjacent direction usually requires building up new abilities and qualifications: the office equipment operation direction needs office process and equipment use experience; the motor and tool repair direction needs motor winding and tool overhaul training; the heavy equipment direction needs hydraulic and power system and large machinery repair experience; the appliance repair direction needs appliance circuit and in-home service experience; the machinery maintenance direction needs servicing system and work order execution experience; and the safety and fire protection system direction needs system installation, acceptance, and compliance training. On-site judgment and measurement habits are transferable, but the qualifications and safety responsibilities of each direction must be obtained again.

entries.answer: Daily work is mainly on-site inspection rounds, emergency repairs, installation, and restocking and cash collection: replenishing merchandise, ingredients, and cash in the machines, collecting coins and banknotes and issuing receipts and settling, inspecting the machines and metering devices to determine the cause of faults and handling banknote or product jams, testing machine functions, adjusting and repairing equipment and replacing faulty mechanical and electrical parts, cleaning and oiling parts, completing the water and power connections for installation per specifications, and keeping maintenance and repair and transaction and cash records. O*NET work context shows 84% have a great deal of decision freedom, 85% use email every day, 53% have daily phone communication, and 51% work more than 40 hours per week.
entries.question: What does a Coin, Vending, and Amusement Machine Servicer and Repairer do every day?

entries.answer: Office equipment operators (except computer) mainly use, operate, and handle clerical affairs; electric motor and power tool repairers focus on servicing motor bodies; mobile heavy equipment mechanics address construction and transport machinery; home appliance repairers address household appliances and on-site service; maintenance and repair workers focus on routine upkeep and do not handle cash or installation; security and fire alarm system installers address system installation, commissioning, and acceptance; this occupation installs, services, and repairs commercial coin-operated, vending, and amusement equipment while also being responsible for cash and merchandise flow. Shared abilities do not mean interchangeability: equipment type, site nature, and compliance requirements differ.
entries.question: Where is the boundary between this occupation and adjacent occupations?

entries.answer: That cannot be inferred. The core tasks of this occupation include on-site judgment of fault causes, deciding whether something can be repaired on site and whether to escalate, confirming wiring and specification compliance, and counting cash and merchandise in person and handling discrepancies; tool output can neither replace these judgments nor remove electrical, equipment, and funds safety obligations.
entries.question: Will AI replace the Coin, Vending, and Amusement Machine Servicer and Repairer?

entries.answer: The earlier-affected parts are the structurable and digitizable steps: manual and drawing lookup, checklist generation, repair record and parts order organization, and aggregation of merchandise, cash, and transaction discrepancies. The later-affected parts are the steps that need judgment and responsibility: judging fault causes and deciding on on-site repair, confirming wiring and specification compliance, handling and escalating book-to-physical discrepancies, and judging site and regulated equipment boundaries.
entries.question: Which tasks are most easily automated?

entries.answer: Judging the actual state of equipment and wiring on site, deciding on de-energization and escalation, holding to safety and counting steps under time pressure, and handling site access and regulated equipment and book-to-physical discrepancy boundaries. These abilities depend on on-site training and acceptance of responsibility.

title.text: Coin, Vending, and Amusement Machine Servicer and Repairer

subject.name: Coin, Vending, and Amusement Machine Servicer and Repairer
subject.summary: Install, maintain, commission, or repair coin-operated, vending, and amusement equipment, including electronic gaming machines, jukeboxes, pinball machines, and slot machines: replenish merchandise, ingredients, and cash in the machines, collect coins and banknotes and issue invoices and settle accounts, inspect the machines and metering devices to determine the cause of faults and handle banknote or product jams, test machine functions, adjust and repair equipment and replace faulty mechanical and electrical parts, clean and oil parts, adjust pressure gauges and thermostats and disassemble and assemble machines per specification, complete the water and power connections for installation per specifications, and keep maintenance and repair and transaction and cash records and discrepancy reporting records.
